newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's ruling party seen losing in state polls.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's ruling party seen losing in state polls.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo's party faces major losses in key elections on Sunday in Mexico's biggest state, a poll published on Friday showed.

The survey in Reforma newspaper showed Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) trailing opposition parties in the four biggest municipalities in the state of Mexico, which votes on Sunday for mayors and state deputies.

The elections, which coincide with similar local contests in the northern state of Coahuila and the poor former mining state of Hidalgo, are the only big test of voter opinion before next July's key midterm congressional elections.

Mexico state's vote will be especially closely watched because its 11.7 million people make up the country's biggest federal unit and because the state -- the heartland of the old Aztec empire -- surrounds Mexico City in a horseshoe shape to the north, east and west.
The main political parties all see the state contest as a dry run for next July's first-ever election of a governor for Mexico City, a post hitherto filled by a presidential nominee.

Noting that the races were close and could still go either way, Reforma's poll showed the PRI would lose the middle-class suburb of Naucalpan to the northwest of Mexico City to the conservative National Action Party (PAN) by a margin of five percentage points.

In the polluted working-class industrial suburb of Ecatepec to the northeast of Mexico City, the poll showed the PAN leading the PRI by one point and in the eastern municipality of Nezahualcoyotl it said the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) led the PRI by one point.
In Tlanepantla, an industrial suburb to the west of Mexico City, the survey showed the PAN leading the PRI by one point.
The survey, conducted on Nov. 5-7, did not give a margin of error.
In Sunday's vote, 122 municipalities will be contested in Mexico state and the PRI, currently holding all but 11 town halls, has the most to lose.

PRI officials blame the dire economic crisis in Mexico and government austerity policies for the falloff in their support. They expect some losses in Sunday's elections but say they will remain the biggest party in all three states voting.
No polls have been published for the Coahuila and Hidalgo state elections but political analysts say the PAN is the main challenger to the PRI in Coahuila and the PRD its main adversary in Hidalgo.
First official results from Sunday's vote are expected late Sunday night or in the dawn hours of Monday.
